story: Fifteen years ago, more than 3,000 Ivorians died because one man, Laurent Gbagbo, would not accept that he had lost an election to Alassane Ouattara. Ouattara came to power as the democrat in that story. In 2026 he began a fourth term at 84, having won it after Gbagbo and banker Tidjane Thiam, the most credible younger challenger, were both struck off the ballot.

The October 2025 vote gave Ouattara nearly 90 percent, but barely half the electorate turned out after the excluded opposition called a boycott and denounced a "civilian coup" (BBC via Africa.com). In December the ruling RHDP took 197 of 255 parliamentary seats (International IDEA). Ouattara got around the two-term limit the same way many leaders in the region have, with a 2016 constitution that, he argues, reset the count to zero. The country he runs is one of Africa's real economic successes: the world's top cocoa producer, with new offshore oil and a mining boom. Political tension is now a question of age rather than ballots. Ouattara has no obvious heir, and the man he once said should hand over to a new generation is still in charge. The 2026 headlines that reached ordinary Ivorians were smaller: 20 people killed by flooding in Abidjan, and a World Cup exit to Norway.
briefing.power: A presidential republic with a strong executive. The president is directly elected for five years and appoints the prime minister, vice president and government; parliament has a National Assembly and an appointed-heavy Senate.
briefing.holders: President Alassane Ouattara (RHDP), in office since 2011.
